newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: INTERVIEW-Swiss Telecom says to keep dominant role.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-Swiss Telecom says to keep dominant role.

text.p: Swiss Telecom expects to lose around 15 percent of its market share for traditional telephone services when the cold wind of competition blows into its home market next year, director general Felix Rosenberg said.
The state group aims to make up lost market share in Switzerland through its foreign investments, he said in a recent interview.
But the focus is on consolidating existing business abroad while preparing for a giant share offering next year.

Rosenberg expressed confidence that investors would flock to buy shares in Swiss Telecom, to be renamed Swisscom in October, despite the wide range of opportunities to invest in other telecommunications privatisations around the world.
"Money will flow into growth sectors and we are the growth sector par excellence," he said.
"Our strategy for 1998 to 2002 is to prove that it pays to invest in Swiss Telecom," he said.
Details are being worked out and will be presented for the initial offering of a minority stake, being coordinated by SBC Warburg and J.P. Morgan.
He declined to give any specific forecasts for sales or profits but said only by stressing growth in these areas could it hope to persuade investors to buy its shares.

Switzerland is throwing open its 10 billion franc ($6.9 billion) telecoms market from January 1, 1998. It already lets private companies offer some kinds of data transmission but Telecom controls most voice transmission and the cellular network.

Telecom's competitors include Newtelco AG -- an alliance of TeleDanmark, Swiss retailer Migros AG, British Telecom and UBS -- and Diax Holding AG, launched by six Swiss electrical utilities with SBC Communications. Swiss Re also has a stake.

"We assume that for traditional services like telephone that we will lose 15 percent (market share)," Rosenberg said. "It depends on how new competitors present themselves and on their development strength."
Telecom has invested two billion francs in overseas operations in developing markets.
"We have invested in the Czech Republic, in India and Malaysia. We are a part of Unisource and are trying to extend our home market into (the German state of) Baden-Wuerttemberg," he said.

"But we also have chances to make profits in a liberalised market as well, and here I am thinking in particular of mobile communications. It is booming enormously in Switzerland. I am also thinking of multimedia, where we can also develop new markets," he said.
The Unisource joint venture also includes PTT Telecom of the Netherlands and Telia of Sweden.
Cost-cutting will also help profits, which slumped to 746 million francs after 681 million in restructuring charges in 1996 from 1.43 billion in 1995, when Telecom took 109 million in charges.
Telecom has already announced it will slash prices in August to prepare for competition and Rosenberg said it was keeping its pricing options open for next year.
"We will of course remain flexible and see what our competitors do, but I cannot really imagine how it can be that prices will be cut in half, as for example Newtelco has said," he said.
Price cuts for international calls are already boosting volume and staving off competition from call-back companies.
"We can see a new development here. Somewhat fewer calls are going via call-back systems because apparently our prices are competitive," he said.
Telecom has been beefing up management by bringing in outside specialists from the private sector. Former IBM executive Tony Reis is now chief operating officer.
"People don't buy assets, they buy management, and this is why we place such great store in having credible people as managers," Rosenberg said.
He painted a picture of Swisscom in five years' time as a streamlined provider of high-quality services whose service would lure back customers from other competitors.
Telephony would remain its biggest source of income and mobile operations would increasingly displace fixed line phones.
Telecom's multimedia role could also grow, he said, although not necessarily via its 32 percent stake in cable television operator Cablecom.
"Swiss Telecom, in future as Swisscom, wants to remain independent. We don't want to delegate an important activity to another company," he said.
The regulatory environment will play a key role in how the market develops, he noted.
"We are not demanding special protection, but we should not be artificially tied down, either," he said.
He said he expected a price to be set by the end of September for competitors to tap into the Telecom network.
"My goal is to come to a mutual agreement....We should find a market-oriented solution and not bother with additional legal measures," he added.
